analysis.one_liner: Requires large meatpackers to buy at least half their cattle through open-market bidding.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan bill with 9 Senate cosponsors that would have forced large meatpackers to bid openly for at least half the cattle they slaughter died in the Senate Agriculture Committee without a hearing or a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required large meatpacking plants to buy at least 50% of the cattle they slaughter each week through "spot market" sales — open, cash-market deals with independent ranchers at a firm price, with a real chance for the rancher to shop competing bids. It also barred packers from counting purchases from ranchers they partly own or control as spot-market sales. The goal was to give cattle producers, who currently sell into a market dominated by a handful of giant packers, more chances to get competing bids for their animals.
analysis.who_benefits: Independent cattle ranchers and livestock producers, especially small and mid-size operations, gain if the bill passes: a large meatpacker would have to come to the open market for at least half of each week's slaughter, instead of filling its plants through contracts and packer-affiliated cattle, which the bill's definitions treat as insider deals. More open bidding means more competition for each animal and a fairer shot at a market price. Rural communities dependent on ranch income share in that gain. States could also go further than the 50% floor, since the bill does not preempt stronger state requirements.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Independent cattle ranchers and livestock producers

how_it_helps.text: Requires each large 'covered packer' to slaughter at least 50% of its weekly cattle volume through spot-market purchases from independent producers, forcing the packer to bid on the open market for half its supply.

Defines a spot-market sale tightly — a firm base price, slaughter within 14 days, and a genuine chance for the producer to solicit bids from other packers — so packers cannot relabel captive-supply arrangements as open-market purchases.

Barred from counting as spot-market sales: any purchase from a producer with a 1% or greater equity stake in the packer (or vice versa), shared officers or directors, or a fiduciary tie to the packer, closing the loophole for packer-owned and affiliated cattle.
Lets states require a higher spot-market percentage than the federal 50% floor, so states that want stronger protections for their ranchers are not held back.

analysis.who_pays: Large meatpacking companies bear the main cost: they would lose the ability to fill half of each week's slaughter from captive supply — their own cattle, contracts, and affiliated producers — and would have to compete for those animals on the open market, likely paying more per head and giving up predictable supply. The industry's argument is that the added procurement cost and volatility could eventually be passed on to consumers in the form of somewhat higher meat prices; that link is contested and was never tested here because the bill never advanced. Small packers with only one plant are exempt, so they bear nothing.
analysis.who_pays_short: Large meatpacking companies and their feedlots

drawbacks.text: The bill covers only beef cattle: it excludes pork, poultry, beef animals over 30 months of age, and foreign-born cattle, so concentration in the hog and poultry industries gets no help from it.

A flat 50% cash-market mandate applies to every covered packer's plant regardless of local conditions, which packers argue would raise their procurement costs and add volatility that could eventually show up in consumer meat prices; the bill offers no flexibility or phase-in.
Small processors are exempt (any packer with only one plant is not a covered packer), so the bill does nothing to build up the small-plant capacity that many ranchers say would help them most.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The upside is real for ranchers: forcing the dominant packers onto the open market for half their cattle directly attacks the captive-supply arrangements that let a few companies quietly set the price of a steer. The honest costs are that a rigid 50% quota could raise packers' costs of doing business, some of which may reach consumers, and that the mandate's carve-outs (no pork, no poultry, no older or foreign-born cattle, no single-plant packers) leave most of the meat industry untouched. The 50% number was never debated or amended in committee, so whether it was the right level went unanswered.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in March 2021 and referred to the Senate Agriculture Committee, which never gave it a hearing, a markup, or a vote before the 117th Congress ended in January 2023, so the bill simply expired.

narrative.text: Sen. Chuck Grassley introduced the bill on March 24, 2021, joined by an explicitly bipartisan group of original cosponsors including Democrats Tester, Smith, Wyden, and Booker and Republicans Hoeven, Ernst, Rounds, and Daines.
The bill was read twice and referred the same day to the Senate Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry, which is where its official record ends.
No further action was ever taken: no hearing, no committee markup, no floor vote. The bill died when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.
Because the bill never passed, no packer was ever required to shift any share of its cattle purchases to the open market.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The large meatpacking companies that dominate cattle buying are better off, because they continue to fill their plants through contracts and affiliated cattle without ever having to bid openly for half of their weekly slaughter. Cattle ranchers, the bill's intended beneficiaries, got nothing.

sides.party_line_note: Support was clearly bipartisan — 9 cosponsors split evenly between 4 Democrats and 5 Republicans, joining Republican sponsor Grassley — but the bill never got a vote, so the partisan shape of the opposition is not in the record.

industries.note: The four dominant packers would have to compete on the open market for at least half of each week's cattle instead of relying on their own feedlots, contracts, and affiliated producers. Their interest in keeping captive supply runs directly against ranchers' interest in getting competing bids.

industries.industry: Packer-affiliated cattle feeding and captive supply
industries.note: Purchases from producers with equity ties to, shared management with, or fiduciary duties to a packer could not count toward the 50% spot-market requirement, sharply limiting the value of packer-owned and vertically integrated cattle. This arrangement is what lets packers set prices without bidding.

industries.industry: Independent cattle ranchers and livestock producers
industries.note: Ranchers would get guaranteed open-market access to the biggest buyers, with a firm price and a real chance to solicit competing bids for their animals. This is the group the bill was written for.

Single-plant packers are exempt from the mandate, so small processors face no new burden while their larger competitors take on the open-market requirement — a relative competitive edge, though the bill does not directly expand their capacity.
